items.stem: How does GraphQL primarily reduce over-fetching compared with REST?

options.text: Clients request exactly the fields they need in a single query
options.rationale: Correct: the client specifies the shape of the response.

options.text: It compresses the HTTP response automatically
options.rationale: Compression is unrelated to the GraphQL model.

options.text: It caches all responses on the server
options.rationale: GraphQL does not mandate server caching.

options.text: It removes the need for a backend database
options.rationale: A data source is still required.

items.explanation: Correct: the client specifies the shape of the response.

items.stem: What problem does a DataLoader solve in a GraphQL server?

options.text: The N+1 problem, by batching and caching related lookups within a request
options.rationale: Correct: it coalesces many per-field lookups into batched calls.
That is handled by the type system/tooling.
Auth is handled via context, not DataLoader.

items.explanation: Correct: it coalesces many per-field lookups into batched calls.

items.stem: Which statements about GraphQL mutations are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Input types group the arguments a mutation accepts
options.rationale: Correct: input types keep mutation signatures tidy and reusable.

options.text: Returning the modified object lets clients update their cache
options.rationale: Correct: returning the payload avoids an extra query.

options.text: A schema may define at most one mutation
options.rationale: False; a schema can define many mutations.

items.explanation: Correct: input types keep mutation signatures tidy and reusable.; Correct: returning the payload avoids an extra query.
